QF.id: AIFM CIII Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_20

question.text: Mr. Vivek Joshi tells his team that portfolios lying to the RIGHT of the market portfolio 'M' on the Capital Market Line represent borrowing at the risk-free rate and investing in the market portfolio. For Himalaya Arbitrage Fund (Cat III AIF) operating under SEBI constraints, what is the MOST important manager-side caveat?

answer.text: Cat III AIFs cannot borrow at all, so the right-of-M region is theoretically inaccessible.
Cat III AIFs face a 2x leverage cap (gross exposure not to exceed 2x of NAV), so the CML can be traversed to the right only up to that limit and at a borrowing rate above Rf.
Cat III AIFs can borrow only from the sponsor, limiting leverage to sponsor commitment.
The CML is irrelevant for Cat III AIFs because they use derivatives, not leverage.

explanation.text: The Logic: CMT allows unlimited risk-free borrowing to scale returns beyond M on the CML (Section 3.12.2). For a Cat III AIF, SEBI (AIF) Regulations impose a 2x leverage cap — the fund's gross exposure cannot exceed twice the NAV. Practically, the CML's right-of-M region is accessible only within this cap, AND actual borrowing rates for Cat III prime-broker financing exceed Rf (prime-broker spread over Repo/MIBOR plus collateral haircut). The Trap: (A) is incorrect — Cat I/II AIFs are zero-leverage; Cat III is NOT. (C) invents a restriction that doesn't exist in the regulations. (D) wrongly separates derivatives from leverage — derivatives DO create leverage; they contribute to the 2x gross cap. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-D (Cat I/II Manager) tests zero-leverage as the defining feature; XIX-E (here) tests the 2x Cat III cap as the counterpoint. XIX-C (All-Cat) tests both. Do not confuse. Manager's Pro-Tip: On a Cat III desk, compute gross exposure daily as (|long MV| + |short MV| + |notional of derivatives|) / NAV. Breaching 2x even intra-day triggers immediate unwind and mandatory reporting. Also factor in prime-broker financing spread when sizing leverage — a 200 bps cost-of-borrow on a 2x book subtracts 200 bps from the CML slope in practice.
